newsitem.title: USA: Dole campaign shelving "Soul Man," publisher says.
newsitem.headline: Dole campaign shelving "Soul Man," publisher says.

text.p: The campaign of Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole has agreed to stop using the classic 1960s song "Soul Man" under the threat of a lawsuit, the song's publisher said on Friday.
The Dole/Kemp campaign told Rondor Music International on Wednesday it would no longer use the song, but it did not concede it had violated copyright, Rondor said.
Dole's campaign had been using, without permission, the soul-music classic with its lyrics changed to "I'm a Dole man."
"We now need to discuss compensation for the past uses," Mary Lee Ryan, Rondor's vice president for business affairs, said. She declined to say how much money she would seek.
A No. 2 pop hit in 1967 for the Stax Records act Sam and Dave, "Soul Man" was written by Isaac Hayes and David Porter.

Rondor announced on Tuesday that it had warned the Dole/Kemp campaign it could be held liable for damages of $100,000 for each unauthorised use of the song, plus legal costs, if a satisfactory settlement was not reached.
The song has been used extensively in the campaign, Ryan said then.
Under copyright law, users of a derivative work, with the same music as an original composition but different lyrics, must pay royalties to the original composers.
